claim: The remedies decision itself (p.108) acknowledges that distributors like Apple will likely still select Google as primary/only default general search engine even with new flexibility.
stance_target: remedy is toothless / Google TAC to Apple is durable
scope_conditions: US v. Google remedies decision, p.108
quoted_support: Even with newfound flexibility, distributors still are likely to select Google as its primary, if not only, default GSE.

claim: Contract terms for default search distribution are shortened to one year (remedies decision p.110), but the author argues this makes no difference because no rival can outbid Google's monopoly-profit-funded offers.
stance_target: annual rebidding is cosmetic, not structurally erosive of Google's rent
scope_conditions: US v. Google remedies decision, contract-term provision
quoted_support: A shorter one-year term for these contracts (page 110 of the remedies decision) makes no difference to Google's ability and incentive to bid for and win these contracts.

claim: The remedies decision (p.110) found that despite Microsoft closing the AI-driven quality gap on desktop search, no new distributor has selected Bing as default and Bing has not gained market share; Neeva, an AI-native search engine, exited the market for lack of distribution.
stance_target: AI entrants (Bing/OpenAI/Perplexity) could realistically bid for and win non-exclusive default placement from Apple soon
scope_conditions: US v. Google remedies decision, discussion of AI competitive dynamics
quoted_support: Microsoft has incorporated AI into its search products, leading Microsoft to believe it has closed the quality gap, at least on desktop. But no new distributor has selected Bing as a default GSE, and to the court's knowledge, Bing has not gained market share because of its product development. Neeva provides another example. It built its search engine on AI technology but ultimately could not compete without greater distribution and left the market. AI has unquestionably improved general search, but it has not yet fundamentally altered market dynamics.

claim: Bing's search index is roughly one-fifth the size of Google's yet achieves comparable search quality on desktop, per the UK CMA's 2020 investigation, suggesting index-size scale advantage is not an absolute barrier to a viable alternative bidder.
stance_target: alternative bidders could feasibly compete for default placement without matching Google's full scale
scope_conditions: UK CMA 2020 market study, Appendix I, para 75
quoted_support: Bing can do this with a search index that is about a fifth of that of Google's (see para 75, CMA 2020, Appendix I: search quality and economies of scale).

claim: Under the EU Digital Markets Act, Google's privacy-preserving data disclosure filters excluded 99% of queries, illustrating how privacy anonymization techniques (also required in the US remedies decision) can gut the practical usefulness of mandated user-data sharing.
stance_target: user-side data sharing remedy is largely ineffective in practice
scope_conditions: EU DMA compliance disclosures, cited in US remedies decision p.161
quoted_support: discussing example of Google's data disclosure under the European Digital Marketing Act where Google's privacy filters resulted in the exclusion of 99% of queries
time_period: as cited in Sept 2025 remedies decision

claim: The syndication remedy only requires syndication on Google's current commercial terms, which the UK CMA found restrict recipients' ability to innovate, change search-result ranking, or use third-party ads -- and syndication partners are ineligible for Google's Android choice-screen remedy.
stance_target: remedy preserves anticompetitive contractual terms rather than eroding them
scope_conditions: UK CMA 2020 Appendix V; US remedies decision syndication provision
quoted_support: the provisions included in these agreements can restrict the ability of recipients to innovate and improve the services they offer consumers, therefore harming competition amongst search engines... companies that have a syndication agreement with Google are not currently eligible to participate in Google's Android choice screen remedy.
